catalog_quote: Finally, Dghweɗe is a tone language with two phonemic tones, H(igh) and L(ow) (Frick 1978a: 9). Apart from coding lexical distinctions, tone in Dghweɗe is used for grammatical ends, e.g. for the coding of imperative mode and for marking the argument structure in VS- and VO-sequences (see section 3.1.1). Prosodically, Dghweɗe utterances are organised in hierarchical layers, the most important of these (for grammatical purposes) being the ‘pause group’ (Frick 1978a: 8): Within the pause group, word-final instances of e are generally omitted and the completive marker –aya is usually shortened to –i. The end of each pause group is marked by polar tone, i.e. a HL- or LH-sequence. However, since a comprehensive prosodic analysis of Dghweɗe is lacking so far, we indicate only surface tones as they occur in actual speech.5 [fn. 5:] In addition, we only indicate tone on recorded material.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dghwede is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical and grammatical tone; the only prosodic domain named is the 'pause group', whose right edge carries a polar (HL or LH) tone. Nothing is said about word stress at all, and the authors state that no comprehensive prosodic analysis exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the passage is explicitly provisional ('a comprehensive prosodic analysis of Dghweɗe is lacking so far').
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated at the word/lexical and grammatical level; the pause-group polar tone is a phrase-level (utterance) phenomenon. The tonal claim is attributed to Frick 1978a: 9 (the verbal-system article), i.e. second-hand; the primary phonology (Frick 1977) was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Dghwede proper (dghw1239, ISO dgh) of the Gwoza hills, Borno State, Nigeria; Hartmann & Zimmermann's data come from one Dghwede consultant (acknowledged in fn. 1) and are given in surface tones only. No dialect distinction is made in any source seen.

sources.locator: Section 2 'Grammatical background', preprint p. 3 (published pagination c. p. 189)
sources.note: Section 2 background (preprint p. 3): Dghwede is a tone language with two phonemic tones H and L (citing Frick 1978a: 9); tone codes lexical and grammatical distinctions; utterances organised in 'pause groups' whose end is marked by polar tone (Frick 1978a: 8); 'a comprehensive prosodic analysis of Dghweɗe is lacking so far'. No statement about word stress (the word 'stress' occurs only once, non-technically, about focus fronting adding 'stress or emphasis').
